title: Houston's Mahatma Gandhi District Is America's Best Indian Food Corridor
excerpt: From Michelin-starred fine dining to $3 jalebi at a 40-year-old sweet shop, Houston's Hillcroft corridor and beyond offer the most diverse Indian food scene in the United States.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Houston's Mahatma Gandhi District is a major hub for Indian cuisine in the U.S.
  • Dining options range from $3 samosas to $110 fine dining experiences.
  • Himalaya and Kiran's are top-rated restaurants in the district.
  • New restaurants are innovating Indian cuisine while respecting traditions.
  • The area serves as cultural infrastructure for the South Asian community.

Article on Houston's Indian food scene
  • Houston's Mahatma Gandhi District along Hillcroft Avenue, officially named in 2010, anchors one of the largest South Asian food corridors in the U.S., serving a metro-area community of over 300,000 residents.
  • The city's Indian dining spans every price point, from Raja Sweets' $3 samosas (open since 1986) to Musaafer's $110 chef's tasting menu inside the Galleria.
  • Chef Kaiser Lashkari's Himalaya, a BYOB institution praised by Anthony Bourdain, and Chef Kiran Verma's eponymous fine-dining restaurant remain top picks among locals and critics.
  • A new wave of modern Indian restaurants — including Kitchen Rumors and Verandah — is pushing the cuisine into bold fusion territory while honoring traditional techniques.

A Culinary Corridor Built by Pioneers

In 1986, Yogi Gahunia opened Raja Sweets on Hillcroft Avenue alongside friends Ramesh Lulla and Aku Patel, who launched neighboring jewelry and clothing shops. The trio called the pocket of southwest Houston "Little India." Four decades later, the neighborhood — officially designated the Mahatma Gandhi District in 2010 — has grown into one of the country's densest concentrations of South Asian restaurants, grocers, and bakeries.

Raja Sweets remains the anchor. Houston's oldest family-owned Indian restaurant operates as both a sweet shop and a casual eatery, drawing crowds year-round for scratch-made mithai, samosas, and pani puri at prices that rarely top $10. During Diwali, the shop overflows with customers purchasing decorative boxes of sweets for gifting.

Across the same strip center corridor, Shri Balaji Bhavan — a father-son operation run by Ramesh and Akash Lulla — serves counter-order South Indian staples. Locals queue for masala dosa, dahi puri, and mixed thalis in a relaxed atmosphere where regulars gather for chai and Madras coffee between shopping trips.

Himalaya: The Institution

No conversation about Houston's Indian food happens without Himalaya. Chef and owner Kaiser Lashkari presides over the cluttered, press-clipping-covered dining room on Southwest Freeway like a host at a permanent dinner party, greeting regulars by name and steering newcomers away from ordering two of the same dish.

"Eating at Himalaya, a classic Pakistani and Indian restaurant in the Mahatma Gandhi District, is a Houston rite of passage."

- The Infatuation

The restaurant's Indo-Pakistani menu rewards strategic ordering. The pepper-heavy chicken hara masala demands a mango lassi chaser. The mutton biryani — gamey, fatty, subtly sweet — pairs with the acidic tomato and cumin notes of the aloo chana masala. Himalaya is BYOB, provided each diner orders an entree and a naan, and has drawn praise from Anthony Bourdain and Andrew Zimmern.

Fine Dining Reaches New Heights

Houston's Indian fine-dining scene has matured considerably. Musaafer, a Michelin-starred restaurant inside the Galleria, seats diners in a space that resembles a luxury Indian palace. Chef Mayank Istwal's menu reflects the flavors of India's 29 states, with highlights like pani puri, tandoori hen, and beef vindaloo. The chef's tasting menu runs $85 to $110, and a sister location recently opened in New York's Tribeca neighborhood.

Chef Kiran Verma, widely described as Houston's "godmother of Indian fine dining," operates Kiran's in the Upper Kirby neighborhood. The restaurant combines traditional ingredients with polished presentation — tandoori duck, wood-fired Texas quail with chutney, and Madras curry. The weekend afternoon tea service, featuring masala chai scones with clotted cream, has become a destination in its own right.

A few blocks away, Verandah — run by husband-and-wife team Sunila and Anupama Srivastava — offers a saffron-infused biryani revealed beneath a flaky pastry crust, alongside duck vindaloo and Bombay fish masala. A seven-to-nine-course tasting menu with wine pairings gives diners the full range.

The Modern Wave

Kitchen Rumors, the latest concept from the Kahani Social Group (which also operates Amrina in The Woodlands), occupies a polished space in the Sixth Ward. The menu pushes boundaries: pani puri arrives with spiced avocado and passion fruit water, the butter chicken ramen reimagines a classic, and dessert includes shahi tukda panna cotta with pistachio and rose. A dog-friendly patio and strong cocktail list make it a date-night draw.

On the casual end, Tarka Indian Kitchen in the Heights serves fast-casual curries, kababs, and garlic naan from scratch at moderate prices, while Pondicheri — helmed by James Beard Award-nominated chef Anita Jaisinghani — pairs a modern counter-service restaurant with an upstairs bake lab serving chai pie and Sindhi laddu.

For the Diaspora: A Taste of Every Region

Houston's Indian dining scene stands apart for its regional depth. Saravanaa Bhavan on Hillcroft brings authentic Chennai-style South Indian vegetarian food. Maharaja Bhog offers bottomless Gujarati and Rajasthani vegetarian thalis. Govinda's, located on the ISKCON temple property in Garden Oaks, serves a daily rotating vegetarian buffet that goes fully vegan three days a week. Aga's, in a southwest Houston strip mall, has built a cult following for its grilled goat chops — five to an order, arriving sizzling on a bed of fragrant onions.

For the Indian diaspora, these restaurants are not just dinner options. They are cultural infrastructure — places to celebrate Diwali, host wedding functions, meet over chai, and introduce the next generation to flavors from home. Houston's South Asian community has spent 40 years building this ecosystem, and the depth shows in every strip center and tasting menu across the city.
